pages.name: Refereeing Spacer
pages.html:
Refereeing Spacer

Spacer is designed to be an open-ended role-playing experience focusing on sandbox gameplay, which can be intimidating for new referees who have never ran or experienced a game like that before. The following outlines how to set up a Spacer game and establish a campaign to help you get started.

Book p.123

pages.name: Creating a Spacer Campaign
pages.html:
Creating a Spacer Campaign

Develop the Subsector: before starting a new Spacer campaign, It is important to make a sub-sector map using the sub-sector map sheet. While some referees may prefer to have the players fully explore and fill in the sub-sector map as they go- this might feel overwhelming for new referees and players.

  • To develop a sub-sector map: see pg. 88 for the procedure. Assume the subsector has typical population density.
  • Player-facing or referee facing?: The map developed can be used as the on-board ship computer library map of the sub-sector with all of the system and planetary data available to the players to help aid with decision making, instead of jumping blindly into the void.

Determine Major Governing bodies within the Subsector: Consider who are the main power groups that have multi-parsec control populating locally. A range of 2-4 (D3+1) power groups is suggested. Typically this represents governments but it could also be megacorps, trade unions, religious organizations, etc.

  • Major Government Details: Write a short sentence that describes the government and three pieces of information that is known to most people within the campaign setting.
  • Use History to help!: If stumped, think about other organizations that have (or currently) exist to help develop some ideas for space-faring empires, confederacies, alliances, etc. You can use the UWC government table as a reference to help develop this as well.

Determine the starting star system and main world: use pg. 90 to determine the main world of each of the neighboring star systems within 2 parsecs.

  • Main World Features: Using the UWC as a reference, come up with three notable pieces of information for each main world within each star system that the ship’s library would have access to.
  • Tech Level: Technology level is important to determine the local manufacturing abilities. For example; if the spacer’s starship breaks down on a planet that is lower tech level than their starship’s M-drive TL. Tech level assumes the locals are aware of higher tech and can only access it via trade, but the referee may want to have the world be isolated and thus has had minimal exposure to interstellar life.
  • Local Flavour: Consider the local customs, life forms, and means of living that would look like on each main world as determined by the UWC.
  • Main World Government Vs. Sub-sector Government: The main world may have a different governing structure than the over-seeing interstellar government the mainworld is a part of to imply a decentralized governing structure. However, the referee can choose to have the local government be the same as the interstellar government.
  • Don't overdo it: 3-5 notes on each world is enough to elaborate on with the worlds.

Create noteworthy NPCs: Develop three different patrons with their own jobs the spacers can interact with, along with three NPCs that the spacers may have contacts with from their prior careers. This can be a police contact, criminal contact, military contact, corporate contact, merchant contact, starport pub owner, etc.

  • Noteworthy NPC locations: Create a location each of these NPCs can be found, with one feature to describe the environment.

Facilitate Character Creation: new spacer players are encouraged to participate in making their characters together, allowing them a way to develop connections between the characters in the emerging narrative of character creation.

  • Walk everyone through their first term of character creation: Walk through the second step of character creation, having each player do each substep simultaneously. Check in with each player to ask what their choice will be and have them roll and explain what each sub-step means (survival, reenlistment, etc.) Players will usually have an idea on the flow of character creation within one or two terms of the character’s career.

Develop as needed: Once you have everything listed above, you have enough information to run a game indefinitely.

  • Expand: as the game goes on, you will need to expand on parts of the sub-sector, add NPCs, factions, etc. Do this as needed based on how the players are steering the game.
  • Improvise: There's no need to flesh out the entire galaxy if the players won’t interact with it. Improvise and use the provided tables if the players drive the campaign in an unexpected direction.

Book p.123

pages.name: Creating a Spacer Adventure
pages.html:
Creating a Spacer Adventure

Creating a Spacer Adventure: Once you have a starmap and notes on each location, the next thing is to develop an adventure for the spacers. Typically spacers are itinerant workers looking to make money across the galaxy. This leaves room for a lot of opportunities for developing adventure ideas.

1) The Incentive

1) The Incentive: Spacers should have an incentive to take on a job that may or may not be risky.

  • Spacer debt: Usually, the main incentive is debt that the spacers are in while paying off their ship. An alternative is the spacer has gambling debt, medical debt, legal debt, etc., if the spacers do not have a starship of their own.
  • Non-debt motivation: External factors may have forced the spacer into the spacing lifestyle, such as escaping conflict, obligations, consequences, etc., that the player can come up with.
  • Rumours: Spacers can interact with locals in a starport or settlement and pick up rumours, which can develop side threads to a campaign that could tie in with their current job or a long-term goal.

2) The Objective

2) The Objective: The referee should develop three starting objectives for the spacers to decide on. A typical way to do this is to develop different patrons offering different jobs.

  • The patron: An easy way to start a spacer campaign is to create a patron who is looking to hire the spacers to perform a job that the patron doesn’t want to do themselves. Patrons may be honest and upfront or may have ulterior motives with the job. Use the patron generation procedures on pgs. 52-55 to help create a patron and then develop their motives.
  • Open-ended: Objectives should be open-ended with various degrees of success or failure based on the character's actions, with unknown information for the players to uncover.

Example of Objectives: You can use the following incentive threads to start a campaign. Elaborate on the details as needed.

  • Transport: Transport a mysterious patron to a mysterious location on a planet. This patron seems to offer more money than normal for this kind of job and seems to be in a rush but won’t tell you exactly where you are headed, just coordinates.
  • Locate: Locate a missing person of interest who has become marooned in the wilderness of a planet. This person is of significant importance to the patron, but they won't disclose why.
  • Investigate: Investigate an old mayday signal in the middle of space, far away from everything. This seems like a routine job for the navy to do, so why is your patron telling you to do it instead of reporting it?
  • Smuggle: Help a person get off or into an amber zone world in a contested part of space. They are offering more than just money, but is it worth the risk?
  • Recover: Something important has gone missing, and you have been tasked with tracking it down within a limited time. If you can’t, there will be consequences!
  • Repo: You are hired as part of a crew looking to repossess a stolen starship that (allegedly) belongs to the patron.

3) The Pressure

3) The Pressure: A spacer adventure should have pressure for the completion of an objective. The standard pressure is financial, but there can also be narrative pressure in the form of consequences for success or failure, such as the effects on the spacer's reputation or NPC relationships, the impact of the loss of time, the consumption of resources, etc.

  • Actions should have consequences: The impact of consequences can be small or large, but there should be a reaction to the spacer’s actions. In addition, inaction is just as consequential as actions. If anything, time is the main resource, and nothing in the campaign should feel static. Making action or inaction important is essential to making a campaign feel lived in.

4) The Drive

4) The Drive: Each spacer is encouraged to have a personal goal that they want to work towards during their campaign. That drive should be one or two sentences and should function as a roleplaying motive for the character. Players are encouraged to create their own. If desired, players can use the Personal Drive table to generate one or use it for examples to develop one.

2DPersonal Drive
2Revenge: You are driven to find catharsis from your pain by doing whatever is necessary to achieve revenge.
3Justice: You have been wronged and seek to even the score to make things right.
4Escape: You seek to disappear among the stars, running away from pain and conflict.
5Survive: Life constantly throws obstacles at you, and you just want to make it to see tomorrow and get by without hassle.
6Freedom: You have always been repressed and stepped on, incapable of escaping your lot in life. Now opportunity has shown you a means to break free.
7Purpose: You have felt aimless, and maybe still do. While your past experiences never fulfilled you, maybe your destiny lies in the stars beyond.
8New Life: You want to reinvent yourself by taking on a life change. In space, you can become anyone you want.
9Wealth: You work tirelessly to seek financial independence, to make life comfortable in your future so you can finally settle down and live a life free of danger. Or perhaps you instead seek wealth for influence, power, or to give charity.
10Faith: You have had a spiritual awakening, discovering the possibility that there is something bigger than yourself out in space that will bring you peace.
11Honour: Your reputation has been blemished in some way, and you seek to fix that.
12Redemption: You haven’t always been a great individual. You have justified your past actions as a means to an end, but now you are driven to right the wrongs you have done.

If using Life events, those could help players develop a personal drive using the events and any generated connections, rivals, enemies, etc., they may have developed.

5) The Appeal

5) The Appeal: Each adventure the spacers embark on should offer something new and exciting for them to interact with beyond just financial incentives. This could include going to new worlds, taking on unique jobs, gaining access to new technology or upgrades, or building narrative connections, such as doing favors for a patron or faction that the spacers can redeem at a later time.

  • Play to the players: The referee should both develop scenarios that play on both the player’s interests as well as their character’s interests, in order to get the players invested in the campaign. The referee can develop different campaign focuses to cater to the different characters, with a primary, overarching focus and then more personalised ones that the characters can follow passively or chip away at.
  • Let players fill in the gaps: As the game starts to take off, players will become more familiar with their characters and their aspirations. This can lead to the players forming connections between unrelated information or plot devices, which should be encouraged to help drive further investment.
  • Throw ideas at the wall and see what sticks: Develop three ideas based on the player’s interests, and see what stands out to them. You may be surprised as to what the players latch onto—thus providing something to develop in the future.
  • Collaborate with players: Let players come up with ideas as they play, and allow them to follow those threads.

6) The Unknown

6) The Unknown: The threads that connect the galaxy together narratively in your campaign should be uncovered over time. Players don't need to know the machinations of the sub-sectorial Technoduke right off the bat, but they would know his name and maybe uncover a thread of corruption tied to him. The mental canon you developed for the sub-sector should not be explained through boring exposition. The players will poke holes at the narrative unknowns or attempt to fill in the gaps between the narrative threads.

  • Mysteries from the mundane: Having a sense of mystery will allow the setting to have unresolved threads the players can latch onto. Mysteries can come up through rumours from NPCs or complications that can occur while completing an objective.
  • Threads should have questions: All threads should offer a question that the players can try to answer through roleplaying actions. Some examples could be how an NPC behaves when asked certain questions, or stumbling across a starship in operational order but missing its crew.
  • Player instincts: As the game unfolds, there will be dynamics that will emerge as the players roleplay their characters and interact with the referee. This can provide the referee with valuable information to help develop a narrative thread. Allowing the players to follow these threads will reinforce their creative thinking and imagination, further driving investment into the game.

Book p.124-125

pages.name: Refereeing Tips
pages.html:
Refereeing Tips

Refereeing Tips: The following is advice I follow that I feel is helpful for new and experienced referees running Spacer.

  • Honesty: Referees should be honest with the players. They should clarify chances of success and frame situations in a way that allows the players to make informed choices.
  • Players drive the game: Players push the game forward, following the ideas that stand out to them. Use them as a main resource for inspiration and guidance in a sandbox campaign. Do not attempt to steer the players into an ideal narrative lane.
  • Deceptive refereeing is bad: Deception will lead to a lack of player investment. If they think they (the person, not by a character they are roleplaying) are being manipulated or intentionally misled by the referee, the players will stop caring and think their choices don’t matter— and this will kill your game. Intentionally tricking players doesn't make you clever; it makes you a bad referee.
  • Explain rules: If something seems unclear to the players, explain it simply with an example to help provide clarification.
  • Frame situations to the players’ lived experiences: In Spacer, the player characters are average people, not heroes. Frame situations to the players by asking them if they think they could do A or if they think the odds of performing B would be successful in real life if they were to do it.
  • Remind players of resources they have: Spacer characters will have equipment or access to resources that can be used to complete tasks. Players may forget what they have at their disposal, so make sure to remind them as needed.
  • Provide the odds of success and failure: Before the players commit, it’s good practice to provide the players with the possible consequences of pass/fail and any gray area if there is a chance for misinterpretation, if the consequences could be significant.
  • Share responsibility: Allow players to name locations, characters, or even help with random generation as needed at the table. Listen to the players discuss ideas, and find inspiration in them.
  • Be fearless and have fun!: Being a referee is exciting and rewarding as long as you remember you're playing a game. You’re a narrator who sets the tone, boundaries, and the spirit of the setting, but you're also a participant in playing the game. Lean into roleplaying NPCs, and use your imagination to weave an engaging narrative.

Book p.125
